introduction: The guide starts from a claim about light: the Prophets do not differ in what they bring, and any apparent difference lies in the receptivity of a changing world. Revelation is measured to capacity, as milk to a child. From this the readings draw a whole account of religious history, in which laws change while a foundation remains, religions age like trees and return like spring, each Messenger promises the next, and no revelation is the last. Much in the older scriptures supports them, and is set beside them here: “I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now”, the law as a schoolmaster, new wine and old bottles, the Qur’an on abrogation, on a messenger for every nation and on words of God that no sea of ink could exhaust, Krishna’s coming from age to age. But every tradition also has its sentences of finality, and they are here too: “Ye shall not add”, a faith once delivered, the Seal of the Prophets, a religion perfected, words that shall not pass away, one mediator. Burke and Santayana speak for what is lost in renewal, Paine and Gibbon for those who doubt revelation altogether, and the Gospel itself for the one who says that the old wine is better.
questions: Revelation, the readings say, is given according to capacity. How do “ye cannot bear them now”, Isaiah’s “line upon line” and Moses shown only what he could bear support that claim, and what does each assume about who decides when capacity has grown?

The readings distinguish an unchanging foundation from laws that change. Test the distinction on “an eye for an eye” and “not one jot or one tittle”, on the sabbath made for man, and on the Qur’an’s verse of abrogation.

Every tradition has sentences of finality: “Ye shall not add”, “the Seal of the Prophets”, “this day have I perfected your religion”, “my words shall not pass away”. How do the readings ask such sentences to be understood, and what would a believer in each tradition reply?
Each Messenger, the readings say, foretells the next. Paul curses any other gospel, even from an angel. How could anyone tell a promised successor from another gospel?

Religions are said to age and need renewal. What do Jeremiah’s old paths, Burke’s cherished prejudices and Santayana’s retentiveness warn against, and does Luke’s “the old is better” deserve sympathy?

All the Manifestations are one, the readings say. How does this differ from Gibbon’s Romans, for whom all religions were equally true, equally false or equally useful, and from Gandhi’s unity in diversity?

outside.why: Any variation in the light of the Prophets, the reading says, “is not inherent in the light itself” but belongs to the receptivity of a changing world. Shelley has the figure for it: one white radiance, and a dome of many-coloured glass.

Each Prophet, the reading holds, was sent with a measure suited to his age. Exodus records such a difference of measure within one tradition: the patriarchs knew God by one name, and another was first given to Moses.

The reading attributes differences between Revelations to “the varying receptivity of an ever-changing world”. The Qur’an gives the simplest case of the principle: every messenger was sent with the language of his own people, to make the message clear.

“All that I have revealed unto thee … hath been in accordance with thy capacity and understanding.” Jesus says the same to his disciples at the end: there are many things they cannot bear now, and another will guide them into all truth.
“Religion … must be living, vitalized, moving and progressive.” Tennyson’s dying Arthur gives the reason in a line: God fulfils himself in many ways, lest one good custom should corrupt the world.

For the reading a religion without motion “is without the divine life; it is dead”. Malachi’s God says “I change not”, and offers that as the ground of His people’s survival. What in religion must not move, if anything is to be relied on?

Each Faith, the reading says, was for centuries a fruitful tree, then “aged … wherefore was it then made young again”. The Letter to the Hebrews draws the same consequence from the promise of a new covenant: what grows old is ready to vanish away.
“Jesus Christ was the real Physician. He appeared, recognized the symptoms and prescribed the real remedy.” The figure is his own, used of himself when he was blamed for the company he kept.

“Milk should be given in suitable proportion, that the children of the world may attain to the station of maturity.” Isaiah describes the teaching of the newly weaned in the same way: precept upon precept, here a little and there a little.
“The veil hiding Our countenance hath not been completely lifted.” Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told that no one can see the face and live; he was shown what could be borne.

Asked why a rite was practised and then abrogated, the reading answers that changing conditions require changing laws. The Qur’an states the principle for its own verses: none is abrogated but that a better or the like is brought in its place.

The reading takes it for granted that a divine law may be set aside when the age changes. Deuteronomy forbids adding to the word that Moses commands. On what grounds could those who received that law accept a later one?
One part of religion “concerns human needs and undergoes change in every cycle”. Jesus says of the most sacred institution of his people that it was made for man, and not man for it.

East and West, the reading says, “have regarded certain customs and conventions as the immutable” basis of religion and neglected its foundation. The same charge is made in the Gospel: the commandment of God laid aside for the tradition of men.
“It is a need and exigency of the time.” Lowell wrote in an American crisis that new occasions teach new duties, and that time makes ancient good uncouth.
The reading recalls that “an eye for an eye” was “converted into ‘Love your enemies’”. This is the passage of the Sermon on the Mount in which the change is made.

The reading describes the stern old law as changed into one of love. In the same sermon Jesus denies that he has come to destroy the law: not a jot or tittle shall pass from it. Is a law that is fulfilled a law that is changed?
“Humanity has emerged from its former degrees of limitation and preliminary training.” Paul uses the same figure for the law of Moses: a schoolmaster, whose charge ends when the pupil comes of age.
“The gifts and graces of the period of youth”, timely then, no longer meet the requirements of maturity. Paul says it of himself: when he became a man he put away childish things.

The reading ranks the stations: Adam the embryo, Christ maturity, and a later perfection. Deuteronomy closes by saying that no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses. How can a tradition honour its founder as unsurpassed and still expect more?

The reading sees the teachings of Jesus as a bud that is only now unfolding. The Letter to the Hebrews also knows a revelation given by degrees, “at sundry times and in divers manners”, but for it the Son is the last word, spoken “in these last days”. What does each take to be finished?

It is correct, says the reading, to call what has appeared wholly new, and correct to call it what was said before. The scribe instructed for the kingdom brings out of his treasure things new and old.
“If God … should today speak a word that all people have spoken heretofore … that word would still be new.” Isaiah’s God announces a new thing and asks whether His hearers will not know it.
The reading insists that a Revelation is new even when its words are old. The Preacher holds that there is nothing new under the sun, whatever is said of it. What would make an old word new?

“The symbols, metaphors, and allegories … can be unveiled, and their true meaning understood.” Daniel was told that he could not understand his own vision: the words were sealed till the time of the end.
“In every century a particular and central theme is … confirmed by God.” The Preacher’s form of the thought is that every purpose under heaven has its season.

The cycle of the Sun of Reality, the reading says, has its seasons, “each brings its vernal season”. The Song of Solomon is the Bible’s spring: winter past, flowers on the earth, the time of singing come.

“Winter arrives—that is, the chill of ignorance and unawareness envelops the world.” Arnold stood on a beach in the nineteenth century and heard such a winter coming, the long withdrawing roar of the sea of faith.
“Each springtime that comes is the return of the springtime that has gone.” Shelley ends his ode to the autumn wind on the same law, as a question he does not doubt.

“When the darkness of winter overshadows them, then again He sends His Messengers.” Krishna says it of himself in the Gītā: whenever righteousness declines he comes, from age to age, to set virtue on her seat again.
“If the religion of Moses had not changed, Christ would not have appeared.” Jeremiah had already spoken, within the old covenant, of a new one not like it.
“If there is no change or alteration, then there is no renewal.” The Gospel’s figure for why the new cannot simply be added to the old is wine and wineskins.

The reading makes change the condition of renewal. The Letter to the Hebrews sets against all “divers and strange doctrines” one who is the same yesterday, today and for ever. What is it that believers need to stay the same?
“The edifice of religion has crumbled … the tokens of certitude blotted out.” Yeats saw the same condition in 1919 and gave it the words by which it is now known: the centre cannot hold.

“All the existing nations had a divine foundation of truth or reality originally.” Paul allows as much of the nations: what may be known of God was shown to them from the creation, and afterwards obscured.

Religions, the reading says, lose their truth with time and “become a body without a soul”. Jeremiah’s image for it is a people who leave a fountain of living water for cisterns of their own that leak.

“Dogmas and codes of human invention are obsolete and barren.” Jeremiah, facing a people eager for something else, tells them to stand and ask for the old paths, where the good way is. When is the remedy a renewal, and when a return?

The reading asks for “new remedies and solutions”, even that “human intellects themselves must change”. Burke defended inherited opinion precisely because it is old: the longer a prejudice has lasted and the more widely it has prevailed, the more he would cherish it. What does a universal reformation risk throwing away?
Lovers of the Sun “perceive the effulgence of the Sun from every mirror” and are not attached to the mirrors. Rūmī says it of lamps: they differ, and the light is the same.
Those who adore the mirror are deprived when the Sun moves to another. Tennyson says of all our systems that they have their day and are “but broken lights” of one who is more than they.

“I am neither of Yathrib, nor of Batha … sometimes in Egypt, sometimes in Bethlehem and Galilee, sometimes in Hijaz.” A voice that claims to have been present in every age is heard in John’s Gospel too: “Before Abraham was, I am.”

In the Manifestation the divine qualities appear “in a form that man is capable of comprehending”. Xenophanes noticed that people give their gods their own form, as oxen would if they could paint. How is a form given for our sake to be told from a form we have made?

The laws “have proceeded from one Source … That they differ one from another is to be attributed to the varying requirements of the ages”. The Qur’an says the difference was willed: for each a law and a way were appointed.
“Moses made a covenant concerning the promised Christ.” This is the promise in Deuteronomy to which that claim appeals: a Prophet like Moses, with God’s words in his mouth.
“Christ made a covenant concerning the Paraclete and gave the tidings of His coming.” The word is from this passage of John, where the Comforter is promised.
The reading traces a chain of promises from Prophet to Prophet. The Qur’an has Jesus himself announce the next link, a messenger to come whose name is the Praised One.

Every Prophet, in the reading, binds his followers to accept the one who comes after. Paul binds his against it: though an angel from heaven preach another gospel, let him be accursed. How would a community that holds both tell a promised successor from another gospel?
“The earth will become another earth.” Isaiah’s promise is of new heavens and a new earth, and of the former things forgotten.

The reading asks whether anyone has heard of a coming “in the clouds of revelation” with manifest sovereignty. Those who watched the Ascension were told to expect a return in like manner as they saw him go. What would they have been looking for?
“This is the Ocean out of which all seas have proceeded, and with which every one of them will ultimately be united.” The Upanishad’s rivers run to one sea and no longer say, I am this river or that.

“All were united with one another—why should we differ?” Pope would end the quarrel another way, by leaving modes of faith to zealots and judging by the life. Does unity come from seeing that the Prophets agree, or from ceasing to care whether they do?

God, the reading says, took a covenant concerning this Cause “in the atoms” of each earlier Book. The Qur’an describes a covenant taken from the prophets themselves: to believe in and help the messenger who would come after, confirming what they held.

“Ye were created for this Day, and concerning this hath God taken a covenant from you.” The Qur’an tells of a covenant older than any Book, taken from all the children of Adam before their birth: Am I not your Lord?

If you believed in Moses, Muḥammad and the Báb because of what was revealed to them, the reading argues, the same kind of verses are before you now. The parable of the rich man makes the argument from the other side: whoever will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded by a wonder.
“All these holy, divine Manifestations are one.” A hymn of the Rig Veda says that the sages give many names to what is One.
The Manifestations “have served one God, promulgated the same truth”. The believers of the Qur’an confess as much: “We make no distinction between any of His messengers.”

The reading holds that all the Manifestations taught the same truth. Gibbon describes another way of treating many religions as one: to the people of Rome all were equally true, to the philosopher equally false, to the magistrate equally useful. What separates the reading’s claim from each of those three?
“When Muhammad came, He declared that Christ was from God and the Gospel was the Book of God.” This is one of the verses in which the Qur’an does so.

The reading speaks of a power that “proves the Truth of Christ to unbelievers after nineteen centuries”. Paine denied that any revelation can be proved to a later person at all: it is revelation to the first and hearsay to every other. What kind of proof would meet his objection?
Asked whether one must believe in all the Manifestations, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes “Had ye believed in Moses, ye would also believe in me.” Here is the saying in its place.
The reading compares the Prophets to successive governors sent by one king. The Gospel’s parable has an owner who sends servant after servant to his vineyard, and at last his son.

“All down the ages the prophets of God have been sent into the world to serve the cause of truth.” The rabbis begin their sayings with the chain as they knew it: Moses to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets.
“The foundation of the divine religions is one.” The Qur’an says that the religion ordained for its hearers is the one commended to Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus.
The fundamental part of every religion, the reading says, concerns morals and the knowledge of God, and does not change. Micah’s summary of what is required is of that part only.

From God’s knowledge “countless Luminaries of learning and wisdom have risen”, and the breath of the All-Merciful has “continually been wafted”. The Qur’an says the words of God could not be exhausted if every tree were a pen and the sea ink.

The Báb warns of a Day when “God shall lift up what He hath sent down and shall reveal other verses”. Most Muslims have read this verse of the Qur’an as closing that possibility: Muḥammad is the Seal of the Prophets. How have those who accept both understood “seal”?

“God ordaineth what He pleaseth”, the reading says, and may send down other verses. The Qur’an records a day on which religion was declared perfected and God’s favour complete. Can what is perfected be followed by more?
The Báb asks his reader whether he ever had any proof of his own religion except the Qur’an itself. The Qur’an makes that argument about itself: is the Book not enough for them?

The reading swears fealty to the Manifestations still to come, “till the end that hath no end”. Emerson told a class of future ministers that their churches spoke of revelation as long ago given and done, “as if God were dead”.

The reading expects revelation after revelation without end. The last page of the Christian Bible warns anyone who would add to its words. Is that warning about one book or about the canon, and what follows either way?

“Abraham … prayed for his offspring, saying ‘O Kind Lord, make my progeny honored and leaders of the world.’” The Qur’an has the prayer, and a condition in the answer: the covenant does not include wrongdoers.
The reading says that Abraham’s prayer for his descendants was accepted. In Genesis the promise is that in his seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.
“In every cycle and age Thou hast ordained a religion for the people of that time.” The Qur’an says it in one sentence: for every nation there is a messenger.

The Báb’s prayer speaks of all earlier religions as abrogated when a new one comes. Gandhi thought the need was not one religion but mutual respect among many, “unity in diversity”. Does succession leave room for the respect he asks?
The new religion “has for its Forerunner His Holiness the Báb”. The Gospel’s forerunner describes his office himself: a voice, making straight the way.

The same reality, says the reading, is called Jesus in one Manifestation and Muḥammad in another. Juliet asks what is in a name, since the rose is the same under any. Why, then, do the names matter so much to those who bear them?
“I was Noah in the day of Noah, and Abraham in the day of Abraham.” Jesus says of John the Baptist, to those able to receive it, that he is Elijah who was to come.

“The Qur’an and all that is therein was created for the Bayán”, and the Bayán for what follows. The Letter to the Hebrews reads the law of Moses in the same forward direction, as the shadow of good things to come.
With Muḥammad, the reading says, “the termination of the prophetic cycle was foreordained”. Jesus marks such a boundary in his own time: the law and the prophets were until John.

God “didst successively reveal the Manifestations” until all previous Revelations culminated in one. The Letter to the Ephesians speaks of a “dispensation of the fulness of times” in which all things are gathered into one.
Moses longed to attain this presence, the reading says, and Muḥammad to behold it. Jesus tells his disciples that many prophets desired to see what they see, and did not.

“Think ye … that the Hand of My … sovereignty is chained up, that the flow of Mine ancient … mercy is checked?” The Qur’an answers those who said that God’s hand is fettered: both His hands are spread wide in bounty.

“If for one moment the tide of His mercy and grace were to be withheld from the world, it would completely perish.” The poet of Lamentations, in a ruined city, says that God’s compassions are new every morning.

“None may ever justifiably claim: ‘We are begotten of the Intellect, while all others stem from another origin.’” Paul tells the Athenians that God made all nations of one blood, and is not far from any of them.
“In every land We have set up a luminary of knowledge.” The Qur’an holds that there is no nation among whom a warner has not passed.

“Revelation is progressive and continuous. It never ceases.” Xenophanes also thought that knowledge grows with time, but put the growth elsewhere: the gods did not reveal all things from the beginning, and by seeking, men find what is better. How much of the progress the reading describes is given, and how much found?

“Past teachings are not suitable for the present time.” Santayana warned that progress depends on retentiveness: where nothing is kept there is nothing to improve. What must a renewed religion retain in order to be a renewal?
“The Spiritual Sun of Truth has always shone from the horizon of the East.” The first people in Matthew’s Gospel to look for the newborn king are wise men from the east, who have seen a star.

“There have been many holy Manifestations of God. One thousand years ago, two hundred thousand years ago, one million years ago.” The Qur’an leaves the list open: some messengers it has told of, and some it has not.
Cycles are “inaugurated, concluded, and renewed, until a universal cycle is completed”. Tennyson ends his long poem looking toward “one far-off divine event, to which the whole creation moves”.

“As the world groweth, so doth the light … and then the Daystar shineth out in noonday splendor.” Proverbs uses the same dawn for a single life: a light that shines more and more unto the perfect day.

The reading sees the dispensations as one growth, each stage connected with the next. Darwin closes his book on a growth of another kind, endless forms evolved from a simple beginning by fixed law. What does the reading’s account of religious history share with his picture, and where does it part from it?
All that had been known before, the reading says, was as two letters, and the rest is now made manifest. Paul describes present knowledge as partial and looks for a time of knowing fully.
“Can a man say, ‘I do not need a new springtime this year—the old springtime is enough for me’?” Tennyson’s bells on New Year’s Eve say the same of the year: ring out the old, ring in the new.

The reading has no patience with one who finds last year’s spring enough. Jesus, having spoken of new wine, adds a sentence of sympathy for him: no one who has drunk old wine at once desires new, for he says, The old is better. What is owed to that attachment?

“A Revelation is totally or partially out of date when it is no longer in accordance with all needs.” Jesus says that heaven and earth shall pass away, but his words shall not. Which part of a Revelation can go out of date, and which cannot?
Each Revelation serves its age and is succeeded. Heraclitus said it of everything: no one steps twice into the same river, for fresh waters are always flowing in.

“The Prophets of God are the Mediators of God”, and one light is in them all. The First Letter to Timothy knows one mediator between God and men. How do those who hold the reading’s view read that “one”?

Every Manifestation gives “a measure of divine guidance ampler than any which a preceding and less receptive age could have received”. The Letter to the Hebrews scolds readers who still need milk when by now they should be taking strong meat.
“It is unjust for the speaker to utter that which is beyond the capacity of his listeners.” Confucius counts it an error in the words to speak to one who cannot be spoken with.

quran-abrogate.text: Nothing of our revelation (even a single verse) do we abrogate or cause be forgotten, but we bring (in place) one better or the like thereof. Knowest thou not that Allah is Able to do all things?

quran-warner-in-every-nation.text: Lo! We have sent thee with the Truth, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner; and there is not a nation but a warner hath passed among them.

quran-praised-one.text: And when Jesus son of Mary said: O Children of Israel! Lo! I am the messenger of Allah unto you, confirming that which was (revealed) before me in the Torah, and bringing good tidings of a messenger who cometh after me, whose name is the Praised One. Yet when he hath come unto them with clear proofs, they say: This is mere magic.

quran-covenant-of-the-prophets.text: When Allah made (His) covenant with the prophets, (He said): Behold that which I have given you of the Scripture and knowledge. And afterward there will come unto you a messenger, confirming that which ye possess. Ye shall believe in him and ye shall help him. He said: Do ye agree, and will ye take up My burden (which I lay upon you) in this (matter)? They answered: We agree. He said: Then bear ye witness. I will be a witness with you.

quran-am-i-not-your-lord.text: And (remember) when thy Lord brought forth from the Children of Adam, from their reins, their seed, and made them testify of themselves, (saying): Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify. (That was) lest ye should say at the Day of Resurrection: Lo! of this we were unaware;

quran-jesus-confirming-the-torah.text: And We caused Jesus, son of Mary, to follow in their footsteps, confirming that which was (revealed) before him in the Torah, and We bestowed on him the Gospel wherein is guidance and a light, confirming that which was (revealed) before it in the Torah - a guidance and an admonition unto those who ward off (evil).

quran-trees-were-pens.text: And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, (were ink), the words of Allah could not be exhausted. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Wise.

quran-seal-of-the-prophets.text: Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets; and Allah is ever Aware of all things.

quran-perfected-your-religion.text: This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion al-Islam

quran-leader-for-mankind.text: And (remember) when his Lord tried Abraham with (His) commands, and he fulfilled them, He said: Lo! I have appointed thee a leader for mankind. (Abraham) said: And of my offspring (will there be leaders)? He said: My covenant includeth not wrong-doers.

quran-every-nation-a-messenger.text: And for every nation there is a messenger. And when their messenger cometh (on the Day of Judgment) it will be judged between them fairly, and they will not be wronged.

quran-hand-is-fettered.text: Nay, but both His hands are spread out wide in bounty. He bestoweth as He will

quran-not-told-thee.text: Verily We sent messengers before thee, among them those of whom We have told thee, and some of whom We have not told thee

quran-same-religion.text: He hath ordained for you that religion which He commended unto Noah, and that which We inspire in thee (Muhammad), and that which We commended unto Abraham and Moses and Jesus, saying: Establish the religion, and be not divided therein

tennyson-old-order-changeth.text: The old order changeth, yielding place to new, / And God fulfils himself in many ways, / Lest one good custom should corrupt the world
tennyson-old-order-changeth.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-broken-lights.text: Our little systems have their day; / They have their day and cease to be: / They are but broken lights of thee, / And thou, O Lord, art more than they
tennyson-broken-lights.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-far-off-divine-event.text: That God, which ever lives and loves, / One God, one law, one element, / And one far-off divine event, / To which the whole creation moves
tennyson-far-off-divine-event.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-ring-in-the-new.text: Ring out the old, ring in the new, / Ring, happy bells, across the snow: / The year is going, let him go; / Ring out the false, ring in the true
tennyson-ring-in-the-new.author: Alfred Tennyson
tennyson-ring-in-the-new.locator: section CVI (CIV in the first edition)

gibbon-equally-true.text: The various modes of worship which prevailed in the Roman world were all considered by the people as equally true; by the philosopher as equally false; and by the magistrate as equally useful
gibbon-equally-true.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-equally-true.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

paine-hearsay.text: It is revelation to the first person only, and hearsay to every other, and, consequently, they are not obliged to believe it
paine-hearsay.author: Thomas Paine

emerson-as-if-god-were-dead.text: Men have come to speak of the revelation as somewhat long ago given and done, as if God were dead
emerson-as-if-god-were-dead.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

xenophanes-by-seeking.text: The gods have not revealed all things to men from the beginning, but by seeking they find in time what is better
xenophanes-by-seeking.author: Xenophanes

avot-chain-of-tradition.text: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.

gita-age-after-age.text: When Righteousness / Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness / Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take / Visible shape, and move a man with men, / Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, / And setting Virtue on her seat again
gita-age-after-age.locator: 4.7–8, in Edwin Arnold’s verse (The Song Celestial)
